newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian defence minister's fate hangs in balance.
newsitem.headline: Russian defence minister's fate hangs in balance.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin held talks on Thursday with a high-flying army general after hastily summoning him from Russia's Far East, heightening speculation he may sack his defence minister in a government reshuffle.
Yeltsin met General Viktor Chechevatov, commander of the Far East military district and a potential successor to Defence Minister Igor Rodionov.
Chechevatov told Interfax news agency they had discussed military reforms and denied he had been offered any new post.

But Russian newspapers said Rodionov's fate hung in the balance after a public rebuke by Yeltsin on Wednesday, although they played down rumours that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin was about to be sacked in a reshuffle expected late next week.
"Rodionov has been warned but not yet fired," the newspaper Kommersant Daily wrote. "The president is starting the search for his successor."

Yeltsin gives few audiences to regional army commanders and the liberal Izvestia newspaper said defence specialists regarded the unexpected meeting as "sensational" and that it could herald big changes in the military top brass.

Izvestia said Yeltsin had been impressed with Chechevatov when he met him last April and that the 51-year-old general had been on the short list of candidates to become defence minister before Rodionov was appointed last July.
Yeltsin told Rodionov on Wednesday to stop "whining" after the minister said he was in charge of "a disintegrating army and a dying navy" and stepped up calls for more defence spending.
But the 60-year-old minister's dismissal is no foregone conclusion. Yeltsin appeared to back him last week and risks more upheaval in the armed forces if he replaces him.

The prime aim of the reshuffle, announced as a measure to improve government social policy, appears to be for Yeltsin to show he is firmly back at the helm after spending most of the last eight months out of the Kremlin with health problems.

Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Wednesday Yeltsin had given no indication about his intentions in the reshuffle, expected after he addresses parliament and the cabinet holds a special session next Thursday.
Yastrzhembsky's refusal to deny any of the rumours floated by the media allowed speculation to continue unabated.

The independent Obshchaya Gazeta newspaper suggested Yeltsin wanted to undermine Chernomyrdin, 58, who has raised his profile by helping ensure relative stability while the president was battling heart problems and then pneumonia.

Yeltsin, wary of jostling for position in the race to succeed him, has often sought to prevent any other single leader gaining too much power and has regularly tried to balance one rival off against another.
But Obshchaya Gazeta and other newspapers on Thursday said Yeltsin would stop short of dismissing his loyal prime minister.

"It is possible that we are dealing with an intentional disinformation leak. Apparently, there is a need to reduce the prime minister's popularity rating which grew during the president's illness," Obshchaya Gazeta said.
"A group of people has gathered around Chernomyrdin who are impatient to make him president. It is also a sign to them: do not be in a hurry..."
